processing: A Ya'an Tibetan tea made by the South Road method of repeated fermentation, then pressed. It carries a noticeable share of stem compared with kang zhuan.
harvest_season: Not defined by a prized picking; like other South Road tea it relies on mature material.
appearance_dry: Deep brown, glossy-dark pressed tea with visible stem.
appearance_liquor: Clear, running from yellowish red to a full transparent red.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf with pieces of stem.
taste_profile: Sweet and smooth on swallowing with a clean aroma, typical of Ya'an Tibetan tea.

brewing.notes: Rinse briefly. It also takes well to simmering in a kettle, the usual approach for Tibetan tea.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and maker, often as aged stock: tea shops offer pieces from the 1970s and 1990s. Traditionally it was packed in large bales for long keeping. Old dates are hard to verify, so buy them from a seller who can explain the provenance.
description:
Jin Jian is one of the named products of Ya'an Tibetan tea in Sichuan, usually mentioned alongside kang zhuan. Despite the English 'Golden Tip', do not expect golden buds: this is a pressed dark tea made for long keeping and everyday drinking.

It follows the South Road method, with its repeated fermentation, and it is then compressed. The easiest difference from kang zhuan is the stem, of which jin jian carries more.

Good examples give a clear red liquor that is sweet and smooth rather than sharp. Rinse it, use boiling water, and if the flat flavour of short steeps disappoints, simmer it.

The tea has traditionally gone out in large bales, and aged pieces turn up from specialist sellers. Read the year and factory on the wrapper, and treat a bargain old lot with suspicion.
history:
Jin Jian grew out of the Ya'an border-tea trade that supplied Tibetan regions, where it and kang zhuan were popular products. Traditional packing was about 30 kg to a package wrapped in cowhide, moved by horse or yak.

When the name itself first appeared is not clearly recorded.
